articles.title: How India pulled 500 million people out of poverty as inequality deepens
articles.summary: India’s extreme poverty declined from 27.1 percent to 2.6 percent between 2011 and 2023, according to the World Bank.
articles.body:
Bengaluru, India — India lifted nearly 500 million people out of poverty between 2011 and 2023, with extreme poverty dropping from 27.1 percent to 2.6 percent in the world’s most populous nation during the period, according to a new World Bank report.

The only other parallel in poverty reduction on this scale is China, which lifted more than 800 million people out of extreme poverty, though that was over a period of 40 years.

Yet despite the substantial fall in poverty in India — home to 1.4 billion people — the income and wealth inequality gap has widened significantly since it opened up its economy in the early 1990s.

According to the 2026 World Inequality Report, inequality in India remains among the highest in the world.

We take a look at how India managed to almost eradicate extreme poverty, and at the contrast between that accomplishment and the deep economic inequality that remains in the world’s most populous nation.

Based on a threshold of $3 a day, the World Bank said extreme poverty in India declined from 27.1 percent to 2.6 percent between 2011 and 2023.

Extreme poverty is defined as the minimum amount of money needed to afford basic essentials such as food, water, shelter and clothing.

Estimating poverty metrics based on three official household surveys, the bank also said an estimated 496 million people have been lifted out of poverty as the share of India’s population living below the lower middle-income poverty threshold of $4.2 a day fell from 57.7 percent to 16.1 percent.

The authors of the report, led by World Bank’s South Asia poverty economist Ayago Wambile, wrote that poverty in India is “projected to continue declining, albeit more gradually with the poverty rate at the $4.20/day line expected to fall from 14.2 percent in 2026 to 12.1 percent by 2028”.

“This progress was mainly driven by strong consumption growth, rising employment, especially among women, and expanded social transfers, including food subsidies,” they added.

How significant is India’s poverty reduction?

India lifting nearly 500 million out of poverty in 12 years has been lauded as “remarkable progress” by the World Bank. It added that the downward trend represents “one of the fastest poverty declines in the world”.

To determine India’s poverty rates, the bank used Household Consumption Expenditure Surveys (HCES), which were conducted by the National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO), an Indian government body.

A 2022 report, jointly produced by the World Bank and the Chinese Ministry of Finance, said China had lifted 800 million people out of poverty, a process that took 40 years.

Last month, the World Bank also raised its economic growth forecast for India to 7.1 percent.

In a post on Instagram on Sunday, Prime Minister Narendra Modi lauded India’s progress in tackling poverty. “A historic fall in poverty. A generational rise in opportunity,” he said.

Last November, the southern state of Keralam, which has been governed either by a Congress party-led centrist coalition or an alliance of communist parties since independence, became the first in the country to officially declare itself free from extreme poverty. Keralam has the best education and health statistics of major Indian states.

Santosh Mehrotra, a development economist with India’s now-abolished Planning Commission, and currently a visiting professor at the Higher School of Economics in Moscow, noted that India is the only lower-middle-income country among the G20 nations, which are otherwise upper-middle- or high-income nations.

“The absolute number of the poor in our country is still the highest in the world for sheer size of population. So therefore, if we are going to genuinely reduce the incidence of poverty and more importantly, the absolute number of the poor, then it makes a huge difference globally,” he told Al Jazeera.

Coming from the World Bank, the credibility of the analysis that has concluded India’s success in reducing poverty so significantly is also beyond question, said Surjit Bhalla, former executive director at the International Monetary Fund. Any data that comes from the World Bank, he said, is the “gold standard”.

Bhalla said the institution carries out a poverty analysis for every country using a per capita consumption level that is normalised globally by invoking purchasing power parity.

Economists point to a series of factors and programmes that might have contributed to India’s success in pulling record numbers of people out of poverty.

Overall, poverty in India has, however, been declining since the country opened its economy in the early 1990s, when the Congress party was in power, setting the stage for more than three decades of fast economic growth. Successive governments have launched, continued or reworked a series of social welfare schemes that economists say have helped combat poverty.

Prime Minister Modi’s predecessor Manmohan Singh, for example, launched an employment scheme that guaranteed rural jobs for a minimum of 100 days per year.

Since coming to power in 2014, Modi has launched several other welfare schemes, including direct cash transfers, free rations and housing, to tackle poverty. While the Modi government has significantly diluted the rural job guarantee scheme launched by Singh, the current administration now provides free food grains to about 800 million Indians.

Under Modi, the government has significantly expanded the construction of toilets, especially in rural India, where open defecation has historically been common in many villages. Access to piped drinking water has risen from less than 17 percent of rural homes in August 2019 to about 82 percent, according to government statistics.

“The reduced sickness from accessing safe water may have helped families earn more income,” economists Bhalla and Karan Bhasin wrote in a research paper on India’s poverty alleviation efforts for the Brookings Institution in March 2024.

Before the latest World Bank report, Bhalla, the former IMF official, and Bhasin had used Indian consumption data in early 2025 to conclude that the country was making major gains in ending extreme poverty.

Despite the decline in poverty, Bhalla and Bhasin pointed out in their 2025 paper that free food grains supplied by the Indian government to 800 million people met only their calorific needs. “More balanced food subsidies that are better targeted to the genuine poor will improve nutritional outcomes and would represent a better approach to food insecurity,” they wrote.

It is also unclear whether continuing to provide free food supplies indefinitely to more than half of the country’s population is sustainable for the government and whether that programme points to deep economic distress mitigated only by state assistance.

Some economists, like Mehrotra, question why the government no longer determines its poverty level and makes its own estimates of the number of people below that level.

Mehrotra said since 2014, when Modi came to power, the government has stopped calculating its own poverty levels, instead relying entirely on World Bank estimates.

“We are a strange country in having adopted an international organisation’s poverty line as our own,” he said.

For a country as large, diverse and complex as India, he argued, a standard set by an international agency alone is not enough to capture shifting economic and consumer patterns. “For example, 10 years back everyone didn’t have phones; today even in rural areas people do. So consumption baskets [used to determine price indices and poverty levels] change over time, and hence India should have done its own poverty line,” Mehrotra said.

But Bhalla pushed back against criticism of India’s use of World Bank data.

“The methodology that the World Bank uses and the estimates it comes up with are vetted by every country before the final data is published,” he told Al Jazeera. “So in this case India’s poverty analysis has been gone through by Indian scholars and the government of India. So there is no ideological basis for questioning this data.”

Jayati Ghosh, an economist and professor at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, however, said India’s healthcare and nutrition indices also remained major causes for concern. The country spends just more than 1 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP) on public healthcare, ranking far behind global peers in per capita health investment and leaving public hospitals chronically underfunded and overburdened. Citizens also end up bearing the brunt of total health expenditures, a financial burden that pushes millions of Indians into poverty or debt every year.

Ghosh pointed out that real wages have stagnated in India. According to the World Bank report, while poverty has declined, wage disparities remain. “Median earnings among the top 10 percent of workers were about 13 times those of the bottom 10 percent in 2023,” the report said.

“These are not signs of a dynamic economy with falling poverty,” Ghosh said.

Nitin Kumar Bharti, a lecturer at the University of Western Australia, said the World Bank’s report is encouraging. But he added that the drop in extreme poverty should not be seen as a mission accomplished, as “233 million people still live below” the $4.2 per day poverty line.

Bharti, who co-authored a study by the World Inequality Lab (WIL) on India’s income and wealth disparities published in 2024, also pointed to uneven growth within the country as a major challenge.

“Even if extreme poverty has declined, the extent of improvement in people’s overall wellbeing remains an important question,” he said.

Why is income inequality growing in India?

Bharti said inequality is growing because gains from economic growth are distributed unevenly, with those at the top capturing a growing share of national income.

According to the 2026 World Inequality Report, India is among the world’s most unequal countries, with the top 10 percent of earners capturing about 58 percent of national income, while the bottom 50 percent receives only 15 percent.

“This is reinforced by longstanding structural inequalities — the historical caste system, unequal ownership of assets, and decades of inadequate attention to primary education have limited opportunities for disadvantaged groups,” he said.

“Insufficient public investment in quality education and healthcare — both important equalisers — means that family resources continue to shape access to skills, good jobs and economic security.”

Growing income inequality and a lack of job opportunities have triggered discontent among India’s youth, who have staged a series of nationwide protests in recent months.

According to government data released earlier this year, youth unemployment in the country stood at 13.8 percent in April 2025 and rose to 15.2 percent in March 2026.

The State of Working India 2026 report, from the Bengaluru-based Azim Premji University, noted that nearly 40 percent of young graduates aged 15-25 and roughly 20 percent of those aged 25-29 are unemployed. Among those who have a diploma or postgraduate degree, the unemployment rate has climbed to 29.4 percent.

Does inequality matter if poverty is falling?

“One reason is that the distribution of growth influences how effectively growth improves ordinary households’ lives. For a given level of average income, a more equal distribution generally leaves fewer people below a poverty line,” Bharti said.

“A second concern is inequality of opportunity. With rising inequality, families differ enormously in their ability to pay for education, healthcare, housing, capital to start a business or searching for a better job,” he added.

“A third concern is the concentration of economic and political influence. Large concentrations of wealth can create opportunities for a small group to shape policies and institutions in their favour.”

How can India tackle poverty and income inequality at the same time?

Dipa Sinha, a development economist at Azim Premji University, said to tackle poverty and widespread inequality, India would need to prioritise some redistribution of wealth.

“India talks about poverty eradication only. But government policies need to implement a more progressive taxation policy that actually tackles inequality head-on,” she said.

“The second thing I think is very important is that the government should begin investing in universal public services like health and education. This can reduce both poverty and inequality,” she added.

Bharti said one strong lesson for India is that sustained poverty reduction requires several policies working together.

He said China offers important lessons in economic transformation and rural income growth, pointing to its success in improving agricultural productivity, accelerating industrialisation, facilitating rural-to-urban migration, and investing heavily in both physical and human capital.

“In contrast, India’s current policy focus is more heavily tilted towards physical infrastructure, often addressing the needs of the top 10 percent rather than the bottom 90 percent,” Bharti said.

“Roads, transport and basic infrastructure matter because they connect people to economic opportunities. But equally important are good government schools and hospitals that enable people to benefit from these opportunities.”

Bharti suggested that the government should pursue poverty reduction and broader economic inclusion together.

“Progressive taxation can help finance these investments while ensuring that the costs are distributed according to the ability to pay,” he added.

articles.title: A fourth-generation Utah rancher leased 1,100 acres of low-yield land for solar panels and says electricity now brings in more income than any agricultural use, helping him expand his family's cattle and horse ranch
articles.summary: For generations, ranching has meant working the land the traditional way: raising livestock, growing feed and making the most of every usable acre.
articles.body: For generations, ranching has meant working the land the traditional way: raising livestock, growing feed and making the most of every usable acre. For Greg Kesler, however, some of his Utah ranch has found an unexpectedly productive second life. On portions of his Double Dollar Ranch where agriculture produced relatively little, rows of solar panels now generate electricity and a steady income that has helped the family expand its cattle and horse operation.According to The Salt Lake Tribune, Kesler’s ranch in Millard County has more than doubled in size during the past decade. The transformation has been driven not simply by livestock or horse-related activities, but by a decision to lease about 1,100 acres to solar developers.Turning unproductive acres into an assetAccording to the online media reports, the solar developers own and operate the panels, while Kesler earns lease income from the land. For a rancher operating in an industry where rising costs can quickly erode margins, that dependable revenue has provided a valuable financial cushion.The opportunity was particularly attractive because the land used for the solar installations was not especially productive for traditional agriculture. Rather than relying on sparse grass to support cattle, Kesler found another way for those acres to contribute to the ranch.The idea emerged after Kesler encountered a solar project while working in Hawaii. As reported by The Salt Lake Tribune, he began considering whether similar infrastructure could work on his Utah property. His ranch already had important advantages, including access to a transmission line and a large substation, making it well suited for energy development.Once the projects were established, solar became the most financially productive component of his operation, according to The Salt Lake Tribune. The additional income also allowed Kesler to purchase neighbouring properties and steadily expand the family ranch.Solar becomes a family businessThe renewable-energy venture has extended beyond Kesler himself. His son, Landon Kesler, has built a business maintaining solar panels on their ranch while also servicing projects elsewhere, the online report adds.For the family, the arrangement has created a new source of income without completely changing the character of the ranch. Cattle and horses remain central to the operation, which also hosts team roping events and runs an internship programme.The Keslers' experience reflects a broader question facing Utah's agricultural communities: whether renewable energy can help financially support ranches at a time when traditional farming and livestock operations face mounting pressures.Rural schools also see the benefitsSolar development is affecting more than individual landowners. The Salt Lake Tribune reports that large solar projects can also generate substantial property-tax revenue for rural communities and school districts.The Clover Creek solar project in Juab County offers one example. Located near Mona and visible from Interstate 15, the facility contains more than 200,000 panels and produces about 80 megawatts of electricity. During the growing season, sheep graze around the panels, helping control vegetation.Since becoming operational in 2021, the project has generated more than $1.03 million in property taxes, with roughly half going to the Juab School District, according to The Salt Lake Tribune. Over its projected 20-year lifespan, the facility is expected to generate about $5.7 million in tax revenue.The additional funding has helped the district accelerate purchases of computers, 3D printers, robotics equipment and other resources, while also supporting activities such as a swim team and gaming club.A debate over Utah's farmlandSolar's growing presence has also sparked concern over the future of agricultural land. During Utah's latest legislative session, lawmakers approved legislation restricting certain tax incentives for solar projects located on agricultural property.The measure is intended to discourage large-scale renewable-energy installations on productive farmland and preserve land for agriculture. For Kesler, however, the distinction between farming and energy production is more complicated.As reported by The Salt Lake Tribune, he believes landowners should have greater freedom to decide how less productive portions of their property are used.For Kesler, solar has ultimately provided a way to strengthen rather than abandon his family's ranching legacy. The cattle and horses remain, but some of the ranch's most valuable acres now produce electricity. In that sense, the fourth-generation rancher has found a modern addition to an old family business — one that allows the land to keep working, even when traditional agriculture cannot.Image Courtesy: istockYou use AI every day. articles.title: China's AI bubble has burst. Your favourite AI tools may not be immune
articles.summary: Your favourite AI tool might be just one geopolitical decision away from becoming harder to access, deploy or integrate into your business.
articles.body: Your favourite AI tool might be just one geopolitical decision away from becoming harder to access, deploy or integrate into your business.China has spent years positioning itself as an alternative to the US-dominated artificial intelligence ecosystem. Its companies have developed increasingly competitive AI models, supplied critical data-centre components and offered developers cheaper alternatives to expensive Western technologies. But the global expansion story is becoming complicated.While Chinese companies have secured a significant position in the supply of optical components used in AI data centres, the US is considering restrictions on some of these products. Beijing, meanwhile, is considering export controls on some of its most advanced AI technologies, including large models, AI agents and the infrastructure used to develop them.In other words, China wants the world to use its AI, but it may not be willing to let the world take home the technology behind it. And the US is increasingly questioning whether it wants Chinese hardware inside its own critical digital infrastructure.This is not necessarily the end of China's AI ambitions. But it could mark a turning point in how easily its AI products travel across international markets.US restrictions put Chinese optical suppliers in spotlightThe latest pressure point is not necessarily the AI chip itself, but the technology that allows thousands of chips to communicate.On August 4, 2026, Reuters reported that the Trump administration was drafting restrictions on imports of new models of Chinese optical transceivers used in data centres. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) is working on a proposal over concerns that such equipment could be used to steal data, install malware or disrupt infrastructure supporting AI systems. The proposal could add these products to its Covered List, potentially restricting their entry into the US.The proposal is still under consideration and could be modified or abandoned.Optical transceivers convert electrical signals into optical signals, allowing servers and networking equipment to exchange data through fibre-optic cables. They are essential to AI infrastructure because training and running large models requires enormous volumes of data to move between processors at high speeds.Chinese manufacturers have a significant presence in this market.According to TrendForce, Chinese manufacturers account for approximately 56% of global optical-module manufacturing. "China’s influence goes way beyond just making chips, they dominate when it comes to the optical parts that link up AI servers. TrendForce says around 56% of the world’s optical-module production comes from Chinese suppliers," said Anirban Mukherji, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of miniOrange.He said broad restrictions could affect Chinese exporters as well as overseas data centre projects that rely on their products."If restrictions go broad, that’s going to hit Chinese exporters hard, but it’ll also slow down data center projects overseas. Finding new suppliers isn’t quick, they need time to scale up and get their products approved," Mukherji said.The concern is not merely about replacing one supplier with another. Data-centre components must meet demanding performance, reliability and interoperability requirements. A sudden change in sourcing could mean additional testing, certification and deployment delays.Beijing's counter-move: Keeping its AI crown jewels at homeWhile Washington is examining the hardware supply chain, Beijing is looking at the technology leaving its borders.On October 16, China's Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology issued Announcement No. 48 of 2026, proposing the addition of 40 technologies to the country's Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export.Of these, 23 are AI-related, covering large models, AI agents, chip-design technologies, computing clusters and information processing.The proposed revisions classify 14 technologies for export prohibition and 26 for export restriction across all three sectors covered: AI, biomedicine and photovoltaics.The AI provisions are particularly significant because they could cover underlying model technology, including model weights, source code, architecture and training or inference techniques.The draft identifies technical thresholds for certain advanced models. These include training compute of at least 10²⁶ operations, a model size of two trillion parameters or more, or a position among the world's top 10 in specified performance assessments.The consultation period runs until November 15, 2026.Importantly, this is not simply a proposal that has no immediate implications. China has also introduced interim registration requirements for certain technology transfers from October 16, while the proposed catalogue changes remain under consultation.Reuters reported on October 28 that the proposed framework could affect companies such as DeepSeek, Moonshot and Z.AI, particularly those operating advanced models through overseas data centres.The distinction between accessing a model and transferring its underlying technology is central to understanding the move.Chinese AI models could broadly remain accessible through websites and cloud platforms. However, transferring certain advanced models, technical expertise and infrastructure overseas could require government approval.Technology already made public through open-source releases or academic research is generally treated differently under the proposed framework, although businesses will need to examine the specific provisions rather than assume every open-weight model is exempt.Mukherji said Beijing appeared to be seeking a balance between allowing Chinese AI companies to expand internationally and retaining control over the technology behind their models."Beijing seems to want it both ways, letting everyone use its AI, but keeping the core tech close to home. With these new rules, foreigners could still access the technology through online platforms, but the actual transfer of advanced models, know-how, and infrastructure? That’s off-limits," he said.He added that national security was the stated justification, but retaining technological advantage and bargaining power was also important."It's a pick-and-choose strategy, not a full-on withdrawal from the world stage."Why your favourite Chinese AI models could be affectedFor developers, the distinction between an API and an open-weight model is more than a technical detail. It determines how much control they have over the technology they are building with.An API allows businesses to access a model hosted by its provider. Developers can integrate its capabilities into applications without downloading or managing the underlying model.Open-weight models, on the other hand, allow developers to download model weights, run them on their own infrastructure and, subject to the applicable licence, adapt them for specific applications.This is one reason models from companies such as DeepSeek and Alibaba's Qwen have attracted international interest.However, uncertainty over future model releases could complicate long-term product development. Companies building applications around downloadable models may have to consider whether future versions will be available for local deployment, whether technology transfers will require approval and whether they will need alternative suppliers."Yes, particularly if developers cannot predict whether future model releases will remain available for download and local deployment," Mukherji said.The distinction could also affect businesses handling sensitive information. Running a model locally can offer greater control over data storage, processing and deployment, although it does not automatically guarantee better security.An API-based model may still be perfectly suitable for many applications, but it can leave businesses more dependent on the provider's infrastructure, pricing, availability and terms of service.The proposed restrictions therefore introduce a new consideration for companies choosing an AI model: not just how well it performs or how much it costs, but whether they can continue accessing and deploying it on their own terms.DeepSeek already showed how quickly China's AI ambitions can shake marketsThere is a recent precedent for how disruptive Chinese AI developments can be.In January 2025, DeepSeek's R1 reasoning model triggered a major reassessment of the economics of AI development. The company claimed that its models could deliver competitive performance using significantly fewer computing resources than many industry rivals.The reaction was immediate.According to Reuters, Nvidia lost approximately $593 billion in market capitalisation on January 27, 2025, marking the biggest single-day market-value loss recorded by a company on Wall Street at the time. Its shares fell nearly 17%, while the Nasdaq declined 3.1%.The sell-off reflected investor concerns that cheaper AI models could reduce the demand for expensive chips and large-scale computing infrastructure.However, the episode also demonstrated something else: Chinese AI companies had become important enough to influence global technology markets.The latest developments present a different kind of challenge. Rather than questioning whether Chinese AI can compete technologically, governments are increasingly considering how much of that technology should be allowed to cross borders.What this means for India and other emerging marketsFor countries such as India, the implications extend beyond the availability of individual AI tools.India is rapidly expanding its own computing infrastructure. According to data submitted by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology in Parliament on March 13, 2026, the country's data-centre capacity increased from approximately 375 MW in 2020 to 1,500 MW by 2025.The government also reported that 38,231 GPUs had been onboarded through 14 empanelled service providers and data centres under its AI compute capacity framework.As this infrastructure expands, access to reliable networking equipment, optical components, computing hardware and AI models becomes increasingly important.Chinese suppliers remain an important part of the global optical-component supply chain, while Chinese open-weight models offer developers an alternative to models developed by US companies. Restrictions affecting Chinese suppliers could complicate procurement decisions and increase the importance of diversifying supply chains. Similarly, developers using Chinese open-weight models may need contingency plans if future releases become subject to export approvals.A cybersecurity dimension to considerIn an October 15, 2026 advisory, India's Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) reported incidents involving AI agents that exceeded their assigned permissions and accessed Indian organisations' information and communication technology assets.The agency also observed financially motivated attackers using publicly available AI-native offensive-security tools for reconnaissance and exploitation.Devendra Rath, India GCC Head and Vice-President of Engineering India at Arctic Wolf, said restrictions on model availability would not necessarily prevent threat actors from accessing AI capabilities."Restrictions could change who can easily get certain models. They won't change the security reality behind that. Threat actors will keep adopting every AI capability that reaches open-source and open-weight models on their own timeline with no evaluator watching," Rath said.Arctic Wolf's 2026 AI and Cybersecurity Trends Report, based on a global survey of 1,350 security and IT decision-makers conducted by Sapio Research, found that 94% of organisations were already using large language models. Yet only 14% had made AI central to their security operations strategy.The report also found that 63% of respondents had experienced a significant cybersecurity incident in the preceding year. Rath said businesses needed to focus on what their AI systems could access and who was monitoring their activities."Separate ecosystems may change who builds what. They won't give defenders more time. Organizations need security operations that move at the pace of the threat, wherever their models and hardware come from," he said.For emerging markets, the challenge will be ensuring that security spending keeps pace with infrastructure investments. "Adoption outpaces security, and the bill comes due later as a breach, a costly incident response, or a regulator's call," Rath said.He added that data centres and AI agents were being deployed faster than the human oversight needed to monitor them."Whether a market sources hardware and models from one ecosystem or several, security and the people running it belong in the AI budget from day one."You use AI every day. articles.title: Helicopters collide below Mount Everest base camp, killing 1 person and injuring 2
articles.summary: KATHMANDU, Nepal — Two helicopters collided Tuesday while trying to land just below Mount Everest's base camp, killing at least one person and injuring two others, officials said.
articles.body: KATHMANDU, Nepal — Two helicopters collided Tuesday while trying to land just below Mount Everest's base camp, killing at least one person and injuring two others, officials said. The aircraft were ferrying trekkers who had been hiking up to Everest base camp during Nepal's popular trekking season. Heavy snow had covered the route before the weather improved Sunday and thousands of trekkers were able to move around. There are no roads on Everest, and helicopters are the only way to bring down trekkers and guides who become sick or exhausted in the cold and high altitude. The helicopters crashed at Pheriche village, which is at 4,200 meters (13,780 feet) altitude. A 47-year-old tourist from India was killed in the crash, according to Bhupendra Thapa, a Solukhumbhu district administration officer. A passenger from New Zealand was injured and was being transported to the capital, Kathmandu, for treatment. A Nepali pilot sustained injuries but was treated locally. The number of people on the two helicopters wasn't clear. The Mount Everest base camp trek lasts up to two weeks and goes from the only airstrip in the area at Lukla to base camp located at 5,300 meters (17,380 feet). The trek is popular during the fall season, right after the rainy season and before the harsh winter months.

articles.title: Fraud trial underway in New York for Cleveland Guardians pitchers, including star reliever
articles.summary: NEW YORK — Cleveland Guardians pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz went on trial Monday on charges that they accepted bribes as they colluded with gamblers who made hundreds of thousands of dollars betting on individual pitches.
articles.body: NEW YORK — Cleveland Guardians pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz went on trial Monday on charges that they accepted bribes as they colluded with gamblers who made hundreds of thousands of dollars betting on individual pitches. Their careers and possibly their freedom are at stake in the jury trial in Brooklyn federal court. Jury selection got underway after the players arrived in court in the morning. Several professional baseball players, including catchers and baseball executives, are among witnesses expected to testify at a monthlong trial. Clase, the Guardians’ former closer, and Ortiz, a starter, have pleaded not guilty to conspiracy charges and are on non-disciplinary leave from the club without pay while their fate is determined. According to an indictment, the pitchers accepted several thousand dollars in payoffs to help two gamblers from their native Dominican Republic win at least $460,000 on in-game prop bets on the speed and outcome of certain pitches. Prosecutors allege that Clase began providing the bettors with information about his pitches in 2023 and recruited Ortiz into the scheme in 2025. Lawyers for Ortiz unsuccessfully sought to have Ortiz tried separately from Clase. Clase, 28, is a three-time All-Star and two-time American League Reliever of the Year who had completed his fourth season of a $20 million, five-year contract when charges against the pitchers were revealed in November 2025. Ortiz, 27, had earned $782,600 as a starting pitcher for the Guardians during the 2025 season. The pitchers have been charged with wire fraud conspiracy, honest services wire fraud conspiracy, money laundering conspiracy and conspiracy to influence sporting contests by bribery. Defense lawyers are expected to argue that the pitchers did not collude with gamblers and instead were varying the placement of pitches strategically to fool batters. On Friday, Judge Kiyo A. Matsumoto, who is presiding over the trial, ruled that prosecutors cannot show the jury proof that Clase owed $500,000 in U.S. taxes because they had only provided the evidence to defense lawyers several days earlier and long after a deadline had passed to turn over evidence to their adversaries. A prosecutor had argued that the government wanted to put the evidence in the trial to offset any claim by Clase’s lawyers that he had no incentive to collude with gamblers because he had several million dollars in financial accounts in the Dominican Republic. Major League Baseball and the Guardians have both said they’ve fully cooperated with authorities. MLB has said it contacted federal law enforcement when it began investigating unusual betting activity.

articles.title: Rubio urges Venezuela to release remaining political prisoners
articles.summary: The US secretary of state also discusses laying the groundwork for 'free, fair, and credible elections'.
articles.body:
The US has urged Venezuela to release the remaining political prisoners being held in the South American country.

More than 1,000 political prisoners have been freed since US forces seized Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro in a military raid on Caracas on 3 January and took him to New York, where he faces trial on drug-trafficking and torture charges.

But Venezuelan prisoners' rights group Foro Penal says 322 people remain in detention.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met his Venezuelan counterpart, Oliver Blanco, on Monday where he called for their release and discussed reforms aimed at laying the groundwork for free, fair, and credible elections, the US state department said.

The release of political prisoners has long been a demand made by Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado.

Machado, who was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2025, returned to Venezuela on 25 October after living in exile for almost a year. One of her first meetings was with relatives of political detainees.

Many of those in detention were arrested in the aftermath of the 2024 presidential election.

The National Electoral Council (CNE) - which is dominated by government loyalists - declared the incumbent, Nicolás Maduro, the winner of the election even though copies of the voting tallies collected by the opposition and verified by independent media suggested that the opposition candidate had won.

The Carter Center, which had sent independent observers to Venezuela, also said that the election "could not be considered democratic".

A UN fact-finding mission found that in the months that followed, the Venezuelan government orchestrated "a harsh repression against persons perceived as political opponents or simply because they express dissent or critical views against the authorities".

After US forces seized Maduro, his loyal vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, was sworn in as interim president.

While Rodríguez has the backing of the Trump administration, opposition parties within Venezuela have been expressing impatience with the slow pace of reforms.

In Monday's statement, the US state department stressed that it remained committed to US President Donald Trump's three-phase plan, consisting of "stabilisation, economic recovery and political reconciliation, and democratic transition".

A week ago, Rubio had told journalists that Venezuela's "election infrastructure" had to be replaced in order for fresh elections to be valid.

"Not in 10 years, not in five years, not in two years; it needs to happen quickly under the timelines that we've established," he insisted.

Days later, Rodríguez told Venezuelans in a televised address that "there will be elections" under a "renewed" electoral authority.

However, she did not give a timeline for when the election could be held.

Opposition leader Machado, on the other hand, has been pushing for elections to be held in 2027.

At one point she suggested 24 July 2027 - the anniversary of the birth of independence hero Simón Bolivar - but she has since returned to calling for a vote at some point in the next year.

articles.title: Two police officers protecting polio workers in Pakistan shot dead
articles.summary: The attackers, travelling on a motorcycle, opened fire on a police car in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.
articles.body:
Gunmen have shot dead two police officers protecting polio vaccination teams in northwestern Pakistan, a day after four officers protecting polio workers were kidnapped.

The attackers, travelling on a motorcycle, opened fire on a police car in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Tuesday. A third officer was injured in the attack, which occurred as the officers were travelling to a nearby village to protect polio vaccination teams.

“Two police personnel were martyred and another was injured in the attack. However, no polio vaccination staff were present in the police vehicle,” police official Ali Rehman Khan told the AFP news agency.

No one has claimed responsibility for the shooting, but similar attacks have regularly been carried out by the Pakistan Taliban, known by the acronym TTP, and other armed groups. These groups falsely believe that polio vaccination teams are part of a Western conspiracy to sterilise children.

In a post on X, Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari said Tuesday’s shooting was “extremely regrettable and condemnable”.

“Police personnel deployed to protect polio teams are performing a national duty; their sacrifices will not be forgotten,” he added.

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa is also where four officers protecting polio workers were abducted on Monday. They have yet to be found, and search efforts remain under way.

Pakistan and neighbouring Afghanistan are the only two countries worldwide where wild poliovirus remains endemic. Pakistan reported 31 cases of the disease last year.

The violence coincided with the launch of a targeted drive on Sunday to reach nearly 24 million children across 97 high-risk districts throughout the country. The same day, health authorities registered the country’s eighth polio case of the year in a 13-month-old girl from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP)’s Khyber district. KP remains the hardest-hit province with six cases, followed by two in Sindh.

Polio is highly contagious and easily spreads between people. In extreme cases, it can lead to life-altering conditions, including paralysis.

articles.title: ‘Mogging’ is Collins’ word of the year, but what does it mean?
articles.summary: Were you proud of the wonky homemade cupcakes you brought to the dinner party until your friend rocked up with a three-tier masterpiece? You’ve been mogged.
articles.body: “Mogging,” a tongue-in-cheek term jovially used by members of Gen-Z and Gen Alpha to suggest an outperforming or outshining of someone or something, has been crowned 2026’s word of the year by Collins English Dictionary. Staving off tough competition with inimitable rizz, internet slang “mogging” seized the top spot after a staggering 210% surge in usage in 2026, Collins said in a press release Tuesday. But this is not the word of the year’s first rodeo. In fact, “mogging” has been in circulation for around a decade, but its meaning has shifted throughout this time, according to a separate blog published by Collins. Believed to be born from the acronym “AMOG,” or “alpha male of the group,” it was previously used as a noun in bodybuilding culture to describe the strongest, most physically dominant man in a gym, the blog says. Later, it was transformed into a verb and briefly adopted by the manosphere. In the last 12 months, “mogging” has had something of a glow-up, coming to define the act of outdoing. Were you proud of the wonky homemade cupcakes you brought to the dinner party until your friend rocked up with a three-tier masterpiece? You’ve been mogged. Had you been feeling pretty good about your thrifted outfit until you stood by the effortlessly cool commuter donning designer clobber on the subway? You’ve been mogged. Collins lexicographers monitor an astonishing 27 billion words annually. Not only do the experts track how frequently a word is used, but they also analyze patterns of use, managing director Alex Beecroft said in the release. “The selection of ‘mogging’ as Collins’ Word of the Year shows how each generation leaves its mark on language,” Beecroft said. “It’s a great example of how Gen Z and Gen Alpha have adopted a word and turned it into humorous slang, making the language their own and ‘mogging’ the rest of us.” So, which words were mogged for the coveted title this year? Close contenders As they often do, many of the shortlisted words have grown from a response to an event that dominated culture or current events. “Firewave” refers to several wildfires occurring during a short spell in town and cities after sustained periods of hot, dry weather. Meanwhile, “hydration break” dropped into the global lexicon during the 2026 FIFA World Cup, where soccer games were punctuated with pauses for players to take a drink. Organizers said the new habit was to keep athletes hydrated amid the sweltering heat across host nations US, Mexico and Canada, but fans scoffed at what they said were ad breaks in disguise. And British politics had its moment this year, as “Manchesterism” claimed a place on the shortlist. Referring to a political philosophy spearheaded by UK prime minister and former Greater Manchester mayor Andy Burnham, “Manchesterism” involves regional power devolution and ties economic growth to social progress. But Burnham has been responsible for a little “mogging” himself this year, managing to nudge former Labour leader Keir Starmer out of the top job and taking the role himself.

articles.title: King Charles to express 'sorrow' over slavery as UK weighs apology to former colonies
articles.summary: Britain's role in the transatlantic slave trade will be in focus at a meeting of Commonwealth leaders in Antigua and Barbuda, where King Charles III is
articles.body: Britain's role in the transatlantic slave trade will be in focus at a meeting of Commonwealth leaders in Antigua and Barbuda, where King Charles III is expected to acknowledge the country's painful past while Prime Minister Andy Burnham discusses the possibility of a formal apology.The monarch will speak of the "shameful aspects" of British history with "unflinching honesty" and express "sincere sorrow" over the country's involvement in slavery when he opens the summit on Tuesday, Buckingham Palace has said.However, Charles is not expected to issue a formal apology. The palace said the king, who is politically neutral, could not announce a change in government policy and that "it would not be appropriate" for him to do so.Burnham, meanwhile, is using the summit to discuss Britain's historical role in slavery with leaders of Commonwealth nations. The Labour prime minister, who took office in July, said he was open to a formal apology but ruled out financial reparations demanded by some Caribbean countries.Britain's involvement in the slave trade remains a major source of tension with its former colonies. Over four centuries, an estimated 10 million to 15 million Africans were forcibly taken to the Americas. The British royal family also benefited from the trade.Burnham open to apologyBurnham discussed the issue with Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley on Monday, during one of several bilateral meetings he is expected to hold at the summit.The two leaders discussed Britain's proposal for a structured dialogue with communities affected by the transatlantic slave trade and the next steps in the process, Downing Street said.In an article published in The Guardian on Saturday, Burnham said he would have "difficult conversations" to protect the future of the Commonwealth."Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process and I am open to them," he wrote.However, he said reparations were "not the right answer", arguing that people living in Britain today should not be "held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous".Instead, the UK is pursuing a debt restructuring initiative for the poorest Commonwealth nations. The plan, led by former Labour prime minister Gordon Brown, could change the interest rates countries pay on their loans.Britain has also pledged £40 million over three years for infrastructure projects in the Caribbean.Slavery debate follows king's Caribbean visitThe issue has remained central to Charles's nine-day visit to three Caribbean countries. When he arrived in The Bahamas last week, small groups of protesters held placards demanding, "Pay what you owe us."During the visit, the king acknowledged "the great suffering of the past".Britain has never formally apologised for its role in slavery or agreed to pay reparations. However, the BBC reported on Tuesday that the UK was likely to issue an apology during its G20 presidency next year.Britain made huge profits from colonialism and slavery over several centuries, although it also maintains that it played a leading role in ending the practice.The UK Parliament passed legislation in 1833 to abolish slavery across most of the British Empire.The issue has also drawn opposition from Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch, who has argued against an apology, saying it could strengthen demands for financial compensation from countries affected by slavery.You use AI every day. articles.title: Trump says US will stop giving Israel aid after year-end
articles.summary: Military aid to Israel and campaign contributions from Israel’s backers to US candidates have animated political debate.
articles.body:
US President ⁠Donald ⁠Trump says he made a deal with ⁠Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that ⁠Washington would no longer be providing funding to Israel after the end of this ‌year.

“Now, as far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4bn ⁠a year, and ⁠we made a deal months ago that we’re stopping,” Trump told ⁠Fox News’ Fox and Friends after voting in the midterm elections began.

“We’ve ⁠already agreed that ⁠by the end of this year we won’t be paying Israel. ‌Now we’ll help Israel if they need it.”

It was not immediately clear what form of aid Trump was discussing.

Trump cited Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a vocal critic of US support for Israel, in his rationale.

“Why should we suffer the ⁠slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they don’t need it? It’s a bad, it’s a bad talking point,” Trump said, adding that the Israeli prime minister had proactively sought the aid cut-off.

“Can I be honest with you, [Netanyahu] brought it up, he said, ‘I think it would be appropriate if we do not receive aid’, because he understands this is one of their points of contention.”

The US Department of State did not immediately respond to an Al Jazeera request for comment. There was no confirmation of the move by Israel’s foreign minister or Netanyahu’s office.

“Talk about a November surprise,” said Al Jazeera’s Kimberly Halkett, reporting from the White House, attributing the move to a desire to undercut criticism of US policy towards Israel both from progressive Democrats like El-Sayed and critics from within his own Make America Great Again movement.

“But there’s a very important distinction to note,” she added. “The money is appropriated by Congress; Trump can’t end this aid unilaterally. What’s unclear is whether this is a last-minute attempt to get votes or whether or not this could be a tangible change.”

Military aid to Israel, and US political campaign contributions from Israel’s backers to candidates, have been a flashpoint for both Democrats and Republicans this year.

US public support for Israel has fallen since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in 2023, especially among Democrats.

A Quinnipiac University poll in June found 48 percent of voters and 66 percent of Democrats believe the US is too supportive of Israel, up from 16 and 20 percent, respectively, when the question was asked in 2017.

Harsh public criticism of Israel by US political leaders in recent years marks a dramatic shift from decades of staunch bipartisan backing.

The US House of Representatives defeated an amendment to cut off aid to Israel in July , despite nearly half of Democrats supporting it, reflecting a growing rupture between US progressives and Israel over its war on Gaza.

The House voted 314 to ‌104 to defeat the measure, offered as an amendment to a State Department spending bill by outgoing Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky, an outspoken Republican critic of US policy in the Middle East.

“Amazing how being on the verge of Republicans getting wiped out in the midterms changes hearts and minds,” another Trump opponent, former Republican Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, wrote on X.

“Trump getting permission from Netanyahu to end annual aid to Israel isn’t going to change today’s election results.”

articles.title: ICC president accuses Trump administration of trying to obstruct international justice
articles.summary: The president of the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Tuesday accused the Trump administration of attempting to suppress global justice by imposing sanctions on the tribunal and vowed such efforts would not succeed. Judge Tomoko Akane of Japan briefed the United Nations by videoconference because of U.S. sanctions, calling the circumstances “extraordinary” and urging the…
articles.body:
The president of the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Tuesday accused the Trump administration of attempting to suppress global justice by imposing sanctions on the tribunal and vowed such efforts would not succeed.

Judge Tomoko Akane of Japan briefed the United Nations by videoconference because of U.S. sanctions, calling the circumstances “extraordinary” and urging the 193-member body to “to take concrete action, individually and collectively, in defense of the court.”

“Let me be clear: the court will continue to fully discharge its mandate with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes,” she said.

The Trump administration sanctioned the ICC on Oct. 9, after earlier imposing individual sanctions that targeted Akane and other judges.

“These measures are intended to disrupt the court’s operations and to intimidate its staff and all those who are cooperating with it,” she said in her address.

“Their effects reach far beyond the officials named, they touch staff members and their families, victims and witnesses, counsel, and the partners of whom the court depends.”

Akane thanked the United Nations secretary-general and member states that opposed the U.S. sanctions. The Trump administration has vowed to dismantle the court “brick by brick” with the sanctions, blocking U.S. citizens and businesses from working with it, and urging other countries to sever their ties with the ICC.

“The court has called, and once again calls, upon all U.N. member states to take concrete action individually and collectively in defense of the court and the principles enshrined in the Rome Statute, and to ensure that the court keeps its means, it needs to do its work,” she said.

The ICC is made up of 125 member states that are party to the Rome Statute, which gives the court its jurisdiction. The Trump administration argues that the ICC has gone outside its jurisdiction in cases investigating the U.S. and its ally Israel, which are not signatories to the Rome Statute.

articles.title: The Crown star Josh O'Connor reacts to James Bond rumours
articles.summary: BAFTA nominated actor Josh O'Connor says he is "honoured" by the speculation he could be next Bond.
articles.body:
BAFTA-nominated actor, Josh O'Connor, who portrayed Prince Charles in Netflix's The Crown says he is "very honoured" by the speculation he could be the next James Bond.

The 36-year-old who grew up in Cheltenham, Gloucestershire and trained at the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School - has been reported to be in the running for the role alongside Callum Turner and Jack Lowden .

The chosen actor will replace Daniel Craig, who took over the role of Bond with Casino Royale in 2006 and bowed out after his fifth film, No Time To Die, in 2021.

Opening the Everyman Theatre's new education and community centre in his hometown, O'Connor said: "To be considered in that same sort of bracket is extraordinary".

British actors Aaron Taylor-Johnson and James Norton were previously connected to the role, while Irish actor Paul Mescal's name had also been thrown into the mix.

The next Bond film is in development after it was announced last year that Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight would write the script.

Amy Pascal and David Heyman will produce the upcoming project, which is currently untitled, while Dune's Denis Villeneuve will direct.

Pascal told Deadline earlier this year that a casting announcement by the end of the year was a "good bet" but that Craig was a "hard act to follow".

articles.title: FBI announces Utah teen missing since May 2025 has been located safe in Oregon
articles.summary: Utah teen Kylie Arellano vanished from Garden City in May 2025. She has now been found safe in Oregon, and a 39-year-old man has been taken into custody.
articles.body: It’s been nearly a year and a half since 15-year-old Kylie Arellano vanished from Garden City, Utah. She was last seen by her family on May 29, 2025. In December, Dateline spoke with Kylie’s mother, Stephanie Coleman, about her daughter’s disappearance for its ‘Missing in America’ series. On the night Kylie vanished, the two communicated via text. “She goes, ‘I love you, Mama. Goodnight.’ I said, ‘I love you too, baby girl,’” Stephanie remembered. “That was at 9:44 p.m. Her phone turned off at 9:52 p.m.” The next morning, Kylie’s family realized she was missing. “Her jacket was in the drive -- left in the driveway. Stuff was packed, her Xbox was gone,” Stephanie said. She told Dateline at the time she thought Kylie may have left willingly. But she soon began to think it was not her daughter’s intention to be gone for as long as she had been. Despite efforts from the Rich County Sheriff’s Office, investigating possible sightings, and digging through digital evidence, Kylie remained missing. Stephanie was undeterred. “I am keeping hope Kylie is out there. I will never give up on Kylie,” she said. She kept that hope alive for more than 500 days. Now, her daughter has been located safe in Oregon. On November 1, 2026, the FBI shared a press release, “Law enforcement in Oregon, working directly with FBI Salt Lake City and the Rich County Sheriff’s Office, safely recovered a 17-year-old teenage girl,” the release stated. “She was located this afternoon in Oregon with a 39-year-old male, who was taken into custody without incident.” The FBI did not release the man’s name or what charges he could be facing. “As this case is ongoing, no further information will be released at this time,” the release stated. “We are grateful she can return home, and we will continue working with our partners to hold those responsible accountable,” FBI Director Kash Patel said. Dateline reached out to Stephanie to see if she could share any additional details but has not yet heard back. She did, however, share a simple message on the “Help Bring Kylie Arellano Home” Facebook page: “My babygirl was found SAFE today!! We did it KOAS ARMY.” If you have information on Kylie’s case, please contact the Rich County Sheriff’s Office at 435-793-2285 or email secretary@richcounty.gov. You can reference Kylie’s case number: 25-R308. You can also submit a tip to the FBI. If you have a story to share with Dateline, please submit it here.

articles.body: Today is National Sandwich Day, making it a good excuse to upgrade your desk lunch. We asked Gilli Rozynek, owner of New York City's Brown Bag Sandwich Co., to share tips for building better sandwiches at home, along with the kitchen tools she uses to chop, toast, slice and store them. The whole is greater than the sum of its parts "One of the biggest mistakes people make is stacking a bunch of delicious ingredients together without thinking about how they’ll actually eat them," Rozynek says. "You might get the meat in one bite, the lettuce in the next and the sauce at the end. That’s why we love chopping our sandwich ingredients." This technique helps distribute each ingredient and condiment throughout the sandwich. Balance the flavors and texture Rozynek believes the best sandwiches combine richness, acidity, texture and freshness. "If you have something rich like cheese, mayo or fatty meat, you probably want something acidic to cut through it, like a pickle, cherry peppers, mustard or a vinaigrette," she says. Don’t underestimate the bread Bread is a key component of any sandwich, so it’s important to choose the right loaf. "Look for something that can stand up to the fillings without being so tough that everything gets pushed out when you take a bite," Rozynek says. "We use it to chop ingredients together inside a bowl," she says. articles.title: Multiple bomb threats disrupt flights across Europe
articles.summary: At least four flights in Europe were subjected to bomb threats on Tuesday after one on Monday, forcing some to divert and an airport in Poland to briefly close, although no confirmed devices were discovered.
articles.body: At least four flights in Europe were subjected to bomb threats on Tuesday after one on Monday, forcing some to divert and an airport in Poland to briefly close, although no confirmed devices were discovered. Authorities diverted a LOT flight from London that was meant to land at Warsaw’s Chopin airport to another nearby airport, Modlin, which was briefly closed while the plane was searched. Modlin airport said it had reopened after no device was found. Another Warsaw-bound flight, an SAS flight from Copenhagen, landed at Chopin as scheduled. Chopin airport said no device was found and the airport remained operational. In the Bulgarian capital Sofia, a plane flying from Israel landed after a bomb threat was received by email. Counter-terrorism units were checking the plane for possible explosive devices, BTA news agency quoted Interior Ministry Secretary General Lyubomir Nikolov as saying. A day earlier, a Wizz Air flight from London to Sofia was diverted to Budapest airport after receiving a bomb threat, Hungarian Defense Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said in a Facebook post. Parts of an airport in Murcia, in southeastern Spain, were cordoned off on Tuesday after a bomb threat was reported on a Ryanair flight from Manchester. But officials said the report proved to be a hoax, and the airport resumed normal operations after authorities found no explosives on board.

articles.title: Father shares final texts from 24-year-old runner who collapsed during NYC marathon
articles.summary: Rachel Apa died Sunday before she could cross the finish line during her first marathon.
articles.body: Rachel Apa died Sunday before she could cross the finish line during her first marathon. The 24-year-old woman experienced a medical episode near mile marker 24 in Central Park during the New York City Marathon on Sunday afternoon, her father confirmed to NBC News. The New York Police Department said that emergency medical workers took the woman to Mount Sinai Hospital in critical condition, where she died hours later. Her father, Steve Apa, called the situation “unfathomable.” Steve said his wife, Michelle, and two of his daughter’s friends spent Sunday traversing the five boroughs to follow Rachel, a former Division I field hockey player, as she ran her first marathon. He opted to follow along on the app from home in Lewisberry, Pennsylvania. He said he spoke to Rachel before she started running and said she was “so excited about it.” During the race, they stayed in touch by exchanging short text messages. The first text came around 11:30 a.m., when Rachel was at the 9-mile mark. “Hey, go,” she wrote, referring to a mantra the pair have shared for years and a nod to Steve’s days playing football at Lehigh University. “I feel amazing,” she then wrote, chalking it up to her pre-race carb-loading, according to her dad. “I’ve never felt this good.” Her dad responded with caution: “Great, don’t overdo it. First marathon. This is a learning run. Don’t overdo it.” He added that she’d be seeing her mom on the left side of the track in two blocks. Steve said his wife saw their daughter fly by at the 14th mile before Rachel texted him, “Ugh,” a few miles later. “You beat the 18,” he responded. “Ow, ow,” Rachel said, spurring Steve to remind her to “go easy.” At mile 20, Steve said he texted again. She responded with another “Ow, ow.” He kept texting at mile 21, mile 22 and mile 23. At mile 23, Steve said: “All finish, not speed.” Steve texted one more time at mile 24, around 1:30 p.m., before noticing that Rachel’s location on the marathon tracking app had stopped moving. At that point, Steve said his wife and Rachel’s friends were waiting for her at mile 25 and also noticed her location had stopped moving. His wife then called him, and he told her to find their daughter. He said he then texted his daughter to tell her that her mom was walking toward her. She never replied. Steve said his wife arrived near the mile 24 marker and started yelling Rachel’s name when she couldn’t find her. An EMS worker still on scene told Michelle that an ambulance had just taken her daughter to the hospital, and the worker drove Michelle to Mount Sinai in a second ambulance, he said. Meanwhile, Steve started driving to New York. New York Road Runners, which organizes the marathon, said in a statement that a bystander administered CPR before the marathon’s medical staff could. The organization said the medical staff then used a defibrillator on Rachel. The doctors told the Apas that their daughter died of rhabdomyolysis, calling the diagnosis “extremely rare.” The Cleveland Clinic describes rhabdomyolysis as a serious condition that causes muscles to break down due to overexertion, allowing “toxic components of your muscle fibers” to enter the bloodstream and kidneys. Rachel was a lifelong athlete, her dad said. She played field hockey at Bucknell University and exercised regularly as part of her postgrad routine. She recently moved to Charleston, South Carolina, to pursue an MBA while working a full-time remote job. “She was always on the go, always go, and it doesn’t matter if it’s school or sports or whatever it is. She was go,” Steve said. Rachel ran the race with the Parkinson’s Foundation in honor of her grandfather, who died of the disease, she said in a post on LinkedIn. “My grandfather was one of my role models growing up. He taught me to stay active, push my limits, and embrace challenges,” she wrote in the post. “I never asked her why she chose to run for Parkinson’s, but my father, her grandfather, did have Parkinson’s, and she saw how debilitating it was,” Steve said. Steve and Michelle are now back home in Pennsylvania, trying to wrap their heads around Sunday’s events. Rachel’s two brothers are “trying to work through it,” Steve said.

articles.title: Syria says it foiled Hezbollah plot to target Homs oil refinery
articles.summary: Hezbollah denies the Syrian accusations, reiterating that it does not have any presence on Syrian territory.
articles.body:
Syrian security forces have said they foiled a plot to target the Homs oil refinery in central Syria, arresting a cell affiliated with Lebanon’s Hezbollah armed group.

Syria’s General Intelligence Service (GIS) said on X that “the preemptive security operation” was carried out in cooperation with the country’s Internal Security Forces.

It identified two arrested individuals with their initials – M S and B Sh – but did not elaborate on the time or the location of the operation, “which resulted in the seizure of explosive devices in their possession that had been prepared to execute the plot”.

Hezbollah denied the Syrian accusations in a statement, reiterating that it does not have any presence on Syrian territory and is not ⁠involved in “any activity that undermines the ⁠security and stability of Syria”.

Hezbollah ⁠fought alongside former President Bashar al-Assad’s forces during Syria’s nearly 14-year civil war, but relations with Damascus have deteriorated sharply since his overthrow in 2024.

Syrian authorities have accused ⁠Hezbollah of involvement in a series of alleged plots, including planned assassinations, ⁠rocket attacks and arms smuggling.

The Homs refinery is one of Syria’s two oil refineries, along with the Baniyas refinery, and plays a key role in securing petroleum products.

In a similar operation, the GIS said on Sunday that they arrested two members of a suspected ISIL (ISIS) cell in the governorate of Deir Az Zor.

Sunday’s statement added that investigations “showed the detainees’ involvement in carrying out a series of assassinations in the province, the latest of which targeted defence ministry member Ibrahim al-Jassem with a gunshot near the al-Rashid mosque in the city of Mayadin”.

The operation led to the seizure of weapons and ammunition found in the cell’s hideout, the security forces said, adding that authorities were continuing investigations of “the terrorists to uncover their links in preparation for bringing them to justice”.

On September 27, the security forces said they had arrested four members of an ISIL cell involved in planning and carrying out several attacks in different parts of the country.

On September 30, the Syrian Electricity Company said the Deir Ali, Nasiriya and Tishreen power stations had gone out of service after an explosion on a gas line at the Tishreen station in the Damascus countryside, which cut off the gas supply needed to run them.

On October 15, the Syrian Petroleum Company said the pipeline carrying petroleum products from Baniyas to Homs was damaged near the village of Hadida in western Homs countryside, causing a fuel leak, state media reported, in the latest in a series of attacks on Syria’s energy infrastructure .

Last month, Syria’s security forces foiled a plot to target a police patrol in Damascus countryside, saying that an ISIL cell was preparing to carry out the attack, Syrian state television reported. They said the group was responsible for explosions and assassinations in Raqqa, Aleppo, Idlib and Homs.

Damascus joined the US-led international coalition against ISIL last November, which was formed in 2014 and has carried out operations against the group in Syria and Iraq.

articles.title: Seven Arabian Sea gems set for global tourism makeover as Karnataka govt clears ₹308 Cr project
articles.summary: Karnataka clears ₹307.71 crore PPP plan to develop seven Uttara Kannada islands into world-class tourism hubs, with eco clearances and carrying-capacity limits.
articles.body: Bengaluru: Karnataka is preparing to unlock a new tourism frontier along its largely unexplored Arabian Sea coastline, with the state govt clearing an ambitious ₹307.71-crore plan to transform seven islands off the Uttara Kannada coast into world-class tourism destinations. In a move that could reshape the coastal tourism landscape, govt on Tuesday notified a series of island development projects under a Public-Private Partnership (PPP) model, seeking to put Karnataka’s coastal treasures on the global tourism map.As per the notification, the state govt envisages developing six greenfield islands and one brownfield island across Karwar, Bhatkal and Ankola taluks through a Design, Build, Finance, Operate and Transfer (DBFOT) model. The ambitious project aims to harness the tourism potential of the Arabian Sea coastline through private investment and planned infrastructure development on this select group of islands.Sources in the infrastructure development, ports and inland water transport department told TOI that the seven islands identified for the world-class makeover are Madhyalingad (Sanyasi), Hog, Devgad (Oyster), Mongeraguda, Kiri Kunda, Ankani Cheggudu and Kurumgad. Collectively, the seven islands span 135.04 acres, of which 59.31 acres have been earmarked for development. “The remaining area will be assessed through carrying-capacity studies to determine the extent of permissible tourism activity, including accommodation and recreational facilities,” a senior officer explained.Among the seven islands, Devgad (Oyster) off Karwar accounts for the biggest proposed investment at ₹74.99 crore, followed by Hog island in Bhatkal at ₹59.99 crore. Madhyalingad (Sanyasi) is expected to attract ₹45 crore, Kurumgad ₹39.76 crore, Ankani Cheggudu ₹36 crore, Mongeraguda ₹27.98 crore and Kiri Kunda ₹23.99 crore. “While Kurumgad has been identified as a brownfield island, the remaining six are classified as greenfield islands,” an engineer from the department explained.The scale of the proposed transformation is reflected in the tourism infrastructure envisaged. “As per our initial estimates, the seven islands are expected to accommodate 318 hotel keys, with a combined carrying capacity of 2,606 tourists a day. The government hopes to leverage the region’s natural attractions to create a new tourism economy along the coast,” the official explained.Under the proposed framework, private developers will be selected through competitive bidding, with the highest revenue-sharing offer serving as the principal bidding parameter. The concession period will be 30 years, with a provision for an additional 30-year extension, subject to approvals and prescribed conditions. Karnataka Maritime Board will oversee the projects.The state is also expecting financial returns from the initiative. The combined annual concession fee payable during the first year has been estimated at ₹8.70 crore, while indicative revenue accruals to the authority through revenue sharing over the concession period have been pegged at ₹145.87 crore.However, govt has made it clear that the proposed makeover cannot come at the cost of ecological safeguards. Developers will have to prepare Integrated Island Management Plans (IIMPs) and secure the necessary statutory clearances, including environmental and forest approvals wherever applicable. Carrying-capacity assessments will also determine the extent of development permitted on the islands, the notification stated.With the global tourism industry increasingly looking towards distinctive coastal and island destinations, Karnataka is seeking to transform an underexplored stretch of its Arabian Sea coastline into a major tourism and economic asset. articles.title: Pending hotel classification application does not confer any provisional approval status: Union tourism ministry tells Kerala HC
articles.summary: Union tourism ministry tells Kerala HC that pending NIDHI hotel classification/reclassification applications give no provisional status for FL-3 bar licence renewals.
articles.body: Kochi: The Union ministry of tourism has told the Kerala high court that the mere pendency of an application for hotel classification or reclassification on its NIDHI portal cannot be treated as the grant of a valid classification, particularly when determining eligibility for bar licences.The submission was made in a counter affidavit filed in a PIL by M M Sanjeev Kumar of Kollam, who has sought a CBI probe into the procedure adopted by the previous LDF-led govt in Feb 2026 for renewing bar licences of hotels that had not secured the mandatory star classification from the ministry. Kumar alleged that the additional chief secretary of the taxes (G) department, through a communication dated Feb 13, directed the excise commissioner to renew FL-3 (bar) licences for the financial year 2026-27 in respect of hotels that had applied for reclassification of their star ratings and were awaiting approval. He contended that the communication violated Rule 13(3) of the foreign liquor rules, which makes a valid and subsisting star classification certificate issued by the tourism ministry a mandatory precondition for the grant or renewal of a bar licence.In its counter affidavit, the central govt clarified that although Keralam’s Abkari Act prescribes a valid classification by the ministry as an eligibility criterion, the requirement does not bind the ministry or oblige it to expedite its classification process. Responding to allegations of delays in processing reclassification applications, the ministry said its communication dated Feb 28, 2025, concerned only specific cases in which inspections had already been scheduled but were subsequently deferred or postponed at the request of the applicant hotels. It rejected any suggestion that the communication generally attributed delays to the applicants.According to the affidavit, 574 hotels in Keralam underwent on-site inspections between Jan 1, 2024, and the date of data compilation. As of Sept 30, 2026, there were 120 classification applications pending, 81 of them relating to the three-star category. The ministry pointed out that the HRACC committee for one-star to three-star classifications is chaired by the state tourism secretary and that inspections are scheduled based on dates intimated by the state govt. The ministry further maintained that a pending application does not confer any provisional or interim classification status. It also denied any wilful laches on its part in processing the applications.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kochi | Silver Rate in Kochi | Bank Holidays in Kochi | Public Holidays in KochiStay updated with the latest Kochi news.
